3 Solving projectile problems: flight time, range, peak

html:
The big picture

Projectile motion, a body thrown at an angle and then left to gravity, is the board's first "2D kinematics problem". With y up, the acceleration is \vec a = (0, -g)^\top: nothing horizontally, -g vertically. Integrating twice, one component at a time, splits the motion into two independent 1D motions sharing one clock: a uniform motion sideways (s_x = v_{0x} t) and a vertical throw up and down (s_y = -g\tfrac{t^2}{2} + v_{0y} t + H_0). The launch velocity enters through its components v_{0x} = v_0\cos\alpha, v_{0y} = v_0\sin\alpha. The three standard questions become simple conditions: the flight time t_F is when s_y = 0 (a quadratic equation), the range is s_x(t_F), and the peak is at t_P, when v_y = 0. The equations only hold between launch and landing.

1 What a projectile is

Lecture: p. 5 · Giancoli §3-7

A projectile is a body that moves freely through the air after it has been thrown, kicked or fired, until it lands: a ball, a stone, a jet of water. The analysis ignores how it was launched and what happens at the landing; only the flight in between counts. Two idealisations are made: no air resistance, and a constant \vec g (heights and distances small compared to the Earth).

Board sketch (p. 5): y up, x to the right. A body is launched from the height H_0 = \ldots\,\mathrm m above the ground (a dotted arrow marks H_0) with the initial velocity \vec v_0 at the angle \alpha = \ldots to the horizontal (circled "1"); the red parabolic path rises, peaks and comes down to the x-axis, where the landing point is marked; "\downarrow g" is circled.

During the flight the only acceleration is gravity, \vec a = \vec g, which is constant. So the motion is uniformly accelerated and the vector law of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall applies:

\vec s = \vec a\cdot\frac{t^2}{2} + \vec v\cdot t + \vec s_0
Symbols
  • \vec s — position vector (m); \vec a — constant acceleration (m/s²); \vec v — the launch velocity \vec v_0 (m/s); \vec s_0 — the launch position (m)
  • t — time since the launch (s)

Under it the board writes: "↑ This EQUATION only works BETWEEN t = 0\,\mathrm s and t_F", where t_F is the flight time, the moment of landing ("F" for flight). Before t = 0 the hand was still pushing; at t_F the ground pushes back and stops the body. In both cases the acceleration is no longer just \vec g. Mathematically the parabola continues below the ground and to negative times (dotted on the board), but those parts describe no real motion; any solution outside 0 \le t \le t_F is thrown away.

2 Horizontal and vertical motion are independent

Lecture: p. 5–6 · Giancoli §3-7

The board writes "\vec s \to 2?": the position now has 2 components (x horizontal, y vertical). A throw stays in one vertical plane, so 2D is enough. Gravity pulls straight down; with y up that is -g in y and nothing in x:

\vec a(t) = \begin{pmatrix} a_x(t) \\ a_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -g \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • a_x(t), a_y(t) — horizontal and vertical components of the acceleration (m/s²)
  • g \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} — magnitude of the gravitational acceleration (a positive number); the minus sign makes it point down

(Without the "no air resistance" assumption, drag would also slow the body horizontally and a_x \neq 0.) Now integrate (\downarrow \int), each component on its own:

\vec v(t) = \begin{pmatrix} v_x(t) \\ v_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v_{0x} \\ -g\cdot t + v_{0y} \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • v_x(t), v_y(t) — horizontal and vertical velocity (m/s)
  • v_{0x}, v_{0y} — components of the launch velocity \vec v_0 (m/s), labelled "INTEGRATION CONSTANT" on the board

The steps: v_x = \int 0\,\mathrm dt = C_1 (nothing changes the horizontal velocity) and v_y = \int (-g)\,\mathrm dt = -g\,t + C_2. At t = 0 the velocity is the launch velocity, so C_1 = v_{0x} and C_2 = v_{0y}: the integration constants are the initial state, which is the board's label. The horizontal velocity never changes; the vertical one drops by 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s} every second. Integrate once more (\downarrow \int):

\vec s(t) = \begin{pmatrix} s_x(t) \\ s_y(t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v_{0x}\cdot t + s_{x0} \\ -g\cdot\dfrac{t^2}{2} + v_{0y}\cdot t + s_{y0} \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • s_x(t), s_y(t) — horizontal and vertical position (m)
  • s_{x0} = s_x(t = 0), s_{y0} = s_y(t = 0) — the launch position (m), the constants of the second integration

Here \int v_{0x}\,\mathrm dt = v_{0x}t + C_3 and \int(-g t + v_{0y})\,\mathrm dt = -g\frac{t^2}{2} + v_{0y}t + C_4; at t = 0 only the constants survive, so they are the launch position.

Choosing the origin on the ground directly below the launch point: the launch is at x = 0, so s_{x0} = 0 (written "\equiv 0" on the board), and at the height H_0, so s_{y0} = H_0. This choice also makes "landing" the same as "s_y = 0".

Splitting the launch velocity. The launch is usually given as a speed and an angle (board):

\vec v_0 = \begin{pmatrix} v_{0x} \\ v_{0y} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v_0\cdot\cos\alpha \\ v_0\cdot\sin\alpha \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • v_0 — launch speed, the length of \vec v_0 (m/s)
  • \alpha — launch angle, measured from the horizontal, upwards positive (° or rad)

Draw \vec v_0 as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with a horizontal and a vertical leg; \alpha sits between the hypotenuse and the horizontal leg, so \cos\alpha = v_{0x}/v_0 and \sin\alpha = v_{0y}/v_0 (the resolving of 2 Vectors and Vector Products). Check: v_{0x}^2 + v_{0y}^2 = v_0^2(\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha) = v_0^2 ✓.

So the two equations of motion are (board, numbered I and II):

\text{I}\quad s_x(t) = v_{0x}\cdot t, \qquad\qquad \text{II}\quad s_y(t) = -g\cdot\frac{t^2}{2} + v_{0y}\cdot t + H_0
Symbols
  • s_x, s_y, v_{0x}, v_{0y}, g — as above
  • H_0 — launch height above the ground (m), the value of s_y at t = 0
Intuition

Gravity only pulls down, so it cannot change the horizontal velocity: sideways the body glides at the constant v_{0x} (equation I, a uniform motion), while up and down it does exactly the vertical throw of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall (equation II). Projectile motion is these two 1D motions running side by side, linked only by the shared clock t. A ball dropped and a ball fired horizontally from the same height hit the ground at the same time.

A ball rolling off a table (right) next to one dropped at the same instant (left). Compare the dots at equal times: they sit at the same height, because the vertical arrows \vec v_y are equal; only the projectile also has the constant sideways arrow \vec v_x. The book's \vec v_{x0} is the lecture's v_{0x}. (Giancoli Fig. 3-20)

The same experiment as a real photo, flashed at equal time steps: red dropped, yellow fired sideways. Every pair lines up on the same horizontal line, so both fall the same distance in the same time. (Giancoli Fig. 3-21)

Special launch directions. Board sketch (p. 7): three launch directions drawn in red from one point: (1) straight up, (2) horizontal, (3) at an angle \alpha (circled); next to them a circled \vec v_0. They are special cases of the same equations, distinguished only by how \vec v_0 splits:

  1. Straight up, \alpha = 90^\circ: v_{0x} = 0, so s_x stays 0: the vertical throw of the cliff example.
  2. Horizontal, \alpha = 0^\circ: v_{0y} = 0; the body only falls while gliding sideways (1 Kinematics › Horizontal throw), and lands after t_F = \sqrt{2H_0/g}, as if dropped from H_0.
  3. At an angle: both components non-zero, the general case.

The circled \vec v_0: together with H_0, the launch velocity decides everything about the throw.

Why is the path a parabola?

Solve I for the time, t = s_x / v_{0x}, and insert it into II:

s_y = H_0 + s_x\tan\alpha - \frac{g}{2\,v_0^2\cos^2\alpha}\,s_x^2

Symbols: as above; \tan\alpha = v_{0y}/v_{0x} (needs \cos\alpha \neq 0, i.e. not a vertical throw).

The height is a quadratic function of the horizontal distance with a negative s_x^2 coefficient: a downward-opening parabola. Eliminating t turns the coordinate–time parabolas of the last lecture into a path.

3 Solving projectile problems: flight time, range, peak

Lecture: p. 6 – p. 7 · Giancoli §3-8

The board lists three questions, with arrows at 1) and 3):

  1. MAXIMUM HORIZONTAL TRAVEL DISTANCE
  2. MAXIMUM HEIGHT
  3. FLIGHT TIME t_F

Board sketch: s_y(t) over s_x(t); the PEAK at t = t_P; the landing point at t = t_F; a dotted line continues the parabola back before the launch.

Each question is one condition on equation I or II:

  • flight time: the body is back on the ground → s_y(t_F) = 0 → solve for t_F;
  • maximum horizontal distance (the range): how far it got sideways by then → s_x(t_F);
  • maximum height: at the peak it moves neither up nor down → v_y(t_P) = 0 → t_P → s_y(t_P).
  1. needs 3) first, which is why the board does the flight time first.

A launch at an angle, with the velocity split at five moments. Watch the dashed arrows: \vec v_x (horizontal) has the same length everywhere, while \vec v_y shrinks, is zero at the peak (the condition v_y(t_P) = 0 used below) and grows downwards after it. The book writes \theta_0 for the lecture's \alpha and x, y for s_x, s_y. (Giancoli Fig. 3-22)

Flight time

s_y(t = t_F) = 0 = -g\cdot\frac{t_F^2}{2} + v_{0y}\cdot t_F + H_0

"ACCEPTABLE t's have to be 0 \le t \le t_F." This is a quadratic equation in t_F, which the board matches to the maths form:

0 = ax^2 + bx + c, \qquad x_{1,2} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
Symbols
  • t_F — flight time (s); x_{1,2} — the two solutions of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (the "midnight formula")
  • here a, b, c are the coefficients of the quadratic, not the acceleration

↓ "MATH / CALCULUS": t_1 = +\ \to\ \boxed{t_F}, t_2 = -. The algebra behind it: the unknown t_F is the maths "x", with a = -\tfrac{g}{2}, b = v_{0y}, c = H_0:

\begin{aligned} t_{1,2} &= \frac{-v_{0y} \pm \sqrt{v_{0y}^2 - 4\left(-\tfrac{g}{2}\right) H_0}}{2\left(-\tfrac{g}{2}\right)} && \text{(insert } a, b, c) \\ &= \frac{-v_{0y} \pm \sqrt{v_{0y}^2 + 2 g H_0}}{-g} && \text{(}-4 \cdot (-\tfrac g2) = 2g\text{; } 2 \cdot (-\tfrac g2) = -g) \\ &= \frac{v_{0y} \mp \sqrt{v_{0y}^2 + 2 g H_0}}{g} && \text{(multiply numerator and denominator by } -1) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Since H_0 \ge 0, the root is at least v_{0y}, so "v_{0y} + \sqrt{\ldots}" is positive and "v_{0y} - \sqrt{\ldots}" negative (or zero for H_0 = 0, the launch moment itself). Only the positive one is acceptable:

t_F = \frac{v_{0y} + \sqrt{v_{0y}^2 + 2 g H_0}}{g}

Symbols as above. For a launch from the ground (H_0 = 0): t_F = 2v_{0y}/g.

Range

"Use t_F → I":

s_x(t = t_F) = v_{0x}\cdot t_F = \ldots\ \mathrm m
Symbols
  • s_x(t_F) — horizontal distance travelled until landing, the range (m)

s_x grows the whole time (v_{0x} > 0 is constant), so it is largest at the last moment the equations are valid, t_F.

Numbers on the board: v_0 = 30\,\mathrm{m/s}, \alpha = 30^\circ, g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} "↑ KEEP IN MIND ITS DIRECTION", and v_0 = \lvert\vec v(t = 0\,\mathrm s)\rvert. "Keep in mind its direction": g is inserted as the positive 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, because equation II already contains the minus sign that makes gravity point down; inserting -9.81 there would make gravity point up. And the given 30\,\mathrm{m/s} is the launch speed, the length of \vec v_0; its components come from \cos\alpha and \sin\alpha.

Unclear (p. 5–6): the board example has no launch height

The sketch writes H_0 = \ldots\,\mathrm m and the results as "\ldots". The example is finished below for a launch from the ground, H_0 = 0, the only reading that needs no extra number. If the tutorial gives an H_0, use the general t_F above.

The board's example finished, with H_0 = 0 (calculator in degree mode):

\begin{aligned} v_{0x} &= 30\,\tfrac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s}\cdot\cos 30^\circ \approx 25.98\,\tfrac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s}, \qquad v_{0y} = 30\,\tfrac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s}\cdot\sin 30^\circ = 15\,\tfrac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s} && \text{(split the launch velocity)} \\ t_F &= \frac{2 v_{0y}}{g} = \frac{2 \cdot 15\,\mathrm{m/s}}{9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}} \approx 3.06\,\mathrm s && \text{(flight time, } H_0 = 0) \\ s_x(t_F) &= v_{0x}\,t_F \approx 25.98\,\tfrac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s} \cdot 3.058\,\mathrm s \approx 79.5\,\mathrm m && \text{(range, equation I)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Units: \frac{\mathrm{m/s}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \mathrm s for the time, \frac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s}\cdot\mathrm s = \mathrm m for the range ✓.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §3-8)

For a launch and landing at the same height (H_0 = 0), inserting t_F = 2v_{0y}/g into I gives the level range s_x(t_F) = \dfrac{v_0^2\,2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{g} = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\alpha}{g} (double-angle identity). It is largest for \sin 2\alpha = 1, i.e. \alpha = 45^\circ, and two complementary angles (20^\circ and 70^\circ) give the same range. Check for the board's numbers: 30^2\sin 60^\circ/9.81 \approx 79.5\,\mathrm m ✓. The formula is wrong as soon as H_0 \neq 0; then use t_F and equation I.

(a) The level range R: launch and landing both at y = 0, the case where the formula holds. (b) The same launch speed at three angles: 45^\circ goes farthest, and 30^\circ and 60^\circ (complementary angles) land at the same spot. (Giancoli Fig. 3-27)

Maximum height

v_y(t) = -g\cdot t + v_{0y}, \qquad v_y(t = t_P) = 0 = -g\cdot t_P + v_{0y} \ \to\ t_P

maximum height: s_y(t = t_P) = \ldots

Symbols
  • t_P — time of the peak (s); v_y(t_P) = 0: at the top the body moves neither up nor down
  • s_y(t_P) — maximum height above the ground (m)

Before the peak s_y increases, so v_y = \dot s_y > 0; after it, v_y < 0. A maximum of a smooth function sits where the derivative is zero, the rule from 3.2 Curve Sketching and Optimization. The board's "\to t_P" and "\ldots" filled in:

\begin{aligned} t_P &= \frac{v_{0y}}{g} && \text{(add } g\,t_P\text{, divide by } g) \\ s_y(t_P) &= -\frac{g}{2}\left(\frac{v_{0y}}{g}\right)^2 + v_{0y}\,\frac{v_{0y}}{g} + H_0 && \text{(insert } t_P \text{ into II)} \\ &= -\frac{v_{0y}^2}{2g} + \frac{v_{0y}^2}{g} + H_0 = H_0 + \frac{v_{0y}^2}{2g} && \text{(}-\tfrac12 + 1 = \tfrac12) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Check with the time-free law vertically: 0 = v_{0y}^2 + 2(-g)\,\Delta y gives \Delta y = v_{0y}^2/(2g) above the launch ✓. With the board's numbers: t_P = 15/9.81 \approx 1.53\,\mathrm s, half of t_F when H_0 = 0 (by symmetry), and s_y(t_P) = 15^2/(2 \cdot 9.81) \approx 11.5\,\mathrm m.

Common mistake — "at the top the velocity is zero"

At the peak only the vertical component is zero. The horizontal component v_{0x} is still there, so the speed at the top is v_{0x}, and the acceleration is still \vec g. Two related slips: putting the full v_0 into the vertical equation instead of v_{0y} = v_0\sin\alpha, and forgetting H_0, which gives the flight time for a launch from the ground.

Worked example — throw from a 15 m wall

A ball is thrown from the top of a 15\,\mathrm m wall at v_0 = 20\,\mathrm{m/s}, \alpha = 35^\circ above the horizontal. Find the peak, the flight time, the range and the landing velocity. (y up, origin on the ground below the launch point.)

  1. Split the launch velocity: v_{0x} = 20\cos 35^\circ \approx 16.38\,\mathrm{m/s}, v_{0y} = 20\sin 35^\circ \approx 11.47\,\mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Peak: t_P = 11.47/9.81 \approx 1.17\,\mathrm s; height 15 + \dfrac{11.47^2}{2 \cdot 9.81} \approx 15 + 6.71 = 21.71\,\mathrm m.
  3. Flight time: t_F = \dfrac{11.47 + \sqrt{11.47^2 + 2 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 15}}{9.81} = \dfrac{11.47 + 20.64}{9.81} \approx 3.27\,\mathrm s (the other root, \approx -0.93\,\mathrm s, is before the launch).
  4. Range: s_x(t_F) = 16.38 \cdot 3.27 \approx 53.6\,\mathrm m.
  5. Landing velocity: v_x = 16.38\,\mathrm{m/s} (unchanged), v_y = 11.47 - 9.81 \cdot 3.27 \approx -20.64\,\mathrm{m/s}; speed \sqrt{16.38^2 + 20.64^2} \approx 26.3\,\mathrm{m/s}, about 52^\circ below the horizontal.
  6. Check vertically with the time-free law: v_y^2 = 11.47^2 + 2(-9.81)(0 - 15) \approx 425.9, so \lvert v_y\rvert \approx 20.64\,\mathrm{m/s} ✓ (the same root as in step 3).
Problem-solving steps — projectile motion
  1. Draw the path; put the origin on the ground below the launch point, x along the throw, y up.
  2. Split the launch velocity: v_{0x} = v_0\cos\alpha, v_{0y} = v_0\sin\alpha; note H_0.
  3. Write I: s_x = v_{0x}t and II: s_y = -g\tfrac{t^2}{2} + v_{0y}t + H_0 (with g = +9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}). Both share the same t.
  4. Translate the question into a condition: landing → s_y = 0; peak → v_y = 0; "reaches a wall at distance d" → s_x = d.
  5. Solve for the time first, keeping only 0 \le t \le t_F; then insert it into the other equation.
  6. Check: units, signs, and the vertical motion with the time-free law.
Connection

The prep course had the same split into a uniform horizontal motion and a vertical throw (1 Kinematics › Projectile motion without drag/friction). Real projectiles also feel air drag, which makes a_x \neq 0; then only the integrals of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall work (drag itself is in 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction).
